title: James Watt was prouder of a set of rods than of any other invention

cover.alt: Looking up at the end of a beam engine's rocking iron beam, with polished rods and links hanging from it.

body: Watt's **double-acting** steam engine pushed its piston with steam both up and down. Earlier engines joined piston and beam with a chain, but a chain can only pull, never push. There was a second problem: the end of the rocking beam swings in an arc, while a piston rod has to move in a straight line. Watt's *parallel motion*, a six-bar linkage, ties the two together, so the piston rod is driven almost perfectly straight up and down while the beam rocks above it.

slides.alt: Seen from below, the end of a beam engine's iron beam rocks up and down while the linked rods hanging from it slide vertically.
slides.caption: A waterworks beam engine built by Harvey's of Hayle: the beam's end swings in an arc, while the linkage keeps the rods below moving straight up and down.
slides.music: “Brandenburg Concerto No. 4 in G, Movement I (Allegro), BWV 1049” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.text: I am more proud of the parallel motion than of any other invention I have ever made.
slides.attribution: James Watt, in a letter to his son, 1808

slides.question: In what year did Watt invent the parallel motion linkage?
slides.explanation: 1784, for his double-acting engine. A simpler linkage in his patent that year was quickly replaced by the parallel motion.

slides.heading: The long road to a straight line
slides.note: The exact straight-line mechanism of 1864 is the Peaucellier–Lipkin linkage

slides.label: roughly how far the linkage's path strays from a true straight line
slides.text: The guided point really traces a tiny piece of a figure-eight curve, but the beam only rocks through a small angle, so that piece is almost dead straight.

slides.question: Why couldn't Watt's double-acting engine keep the old chain?
options: A chain can pull but not push
slides.explanation: Steam now drove the piston both ways, so the link to the beam had to push as well as pull, and keep the rod straight while doing it.
